opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
“The chosen one at Babylon sends you greetings, as does Mark, my son.”

I never quite understood this passage. It feels small, almost casual, yet it carries the weight of an entire moment in time. This was the early Church—after Christ had ascended, after they had been anointed with the Holy Spirit—moving, building, and spreading the Word under constant pressure. They traveled far, made disciples, and lived under the scrutiny of both Rome and certain Jewish authorities of the time.

They even had to speak in a kind of camouflage. “Babylon” was not just a place—it was a code. A name for Rome. A way of saying: we are here, inside a powerful and hostile system, and yet we remain faithful.

So this simple line—“the chosen one at Babylon”—is not just a greeting. It is the Church speaking to the Church. A quiet but steady declaration: we are still here.

And Mark, “my son”—this is John Mark, the one traditionally linked to the Gospel of Mark. Not a son by blood, but by faith. A disciple. A continuation.

What a time that must have been—faith under pressure, unity across distance, and spiritual lineage forming just as Christ had instructed.

And it did not end there.

It lives on today. Maybe not in camouflage, but in the same truth:
we are still here, still connected, still chosen—no matter where we are planted.
